title: Factcheck: UK Conservatives double the ‘cost of net-zero’ after spreadsheet blunder - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief finds the UK Conservatives' 'Right Way' booklet claims net-zero would cost £957bn per the CCC, but that figure double-counts a 2020 CCC spreadsheet whose real net total is £478bn; the CCC's 2025 revision cut it to £108bn (<0.2% of GDP), largely due to cheaper EVs. The error traces from David Turver's January 2026 Spectator/IEA pieces via the Great British Think Tank.

insights.claim: The Conservative 'Right Way' document claims the CCC estimated in 2020 that net-zero would cost £957bn, but the CCC's 2020 estimate was exactly half that, £478bn.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Headline net-zero cost claims in UK politics can be off by 2x; investors should verify primary sources before pricing policy risk.
insights.quote: In fact, the CCC’s 2020 estimate was exactly half this amount – £478bn

insights.claim: The CCC's 2020 spreadsheet shows £1.38tn of extra capex over 2020-50 offset by £0.90tn of operating savings, netting £478bn.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Net-zero is capex-heavy but largely self-financing via opex savings, supporting low-carbon investment theses.

insights.claim: In 2025 the CCC revised net-zero investment costs to £670bn and operating savings to £562bn, a net £108bn over 2025-50 or under 0.2% of GDP, mainly because of falling electric vehicle costs.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Falling EV costs are sharply reducing the estimated macro cost of UK decarbonisation.
insights.locator: In 2025, the CCC revised its estimates

insights.claim: In 2020 the CCC said the £478bn net cost was under 1% of GDP over 30 years and that the investment would boost GDP by around 2% via lower fossil-fuel imports.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Official UK modelling frames net-zero as a net GDP positive, relevant to UK macro and energy-transition positioning.
insights.locator: At the time of publication in 2020

insights.claim: The CCC said this year that reaching net-zero would cost less than a single fossil-fuel price shock and would deliver benefits worth £110bn per year.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Framing decarbonisation as energy-security hedge strengthens the policy case for UK clean energy buildout.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, the committee said

insights.claim: The £957bn figure appears to result from summing every number in the CCC spreadsheet including its existing annual-total line, double-counting both costs and savings.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: A simple spreadsheet error is shaping opposition party energy policy narrative.

insights.claim: The earliest online use of £957bn was a 12 January 2026 Spectator article by David Turver, repeated a day later in his Institute of Economic Affairs report, then by the Great British Think Tank in March, before appearing in the Conservative document in October 2026.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Shows how flawed cost figures propagate through think-tank networks into party platforms.

insights.claim: Turver's report also spawned headlines that net-zero would cost £7.6tn or even £9tn, figures implicitly assuming fossil fuels and the cars, boilers and power plants using them are free.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Gross-cost headlines ignoring counterfactual spending distort the UK net-zero debate and policy risk perception.

insights.claim: The Conservative booklet argues political judgement should not be substituted by sophisticated modelling while itself relying on a miscalculated figure.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Signals UK Conservatives are positioning against net-zero spending, a political risk for UK clean-energy investments if they regain power.
